beats.narration_text: Someone assumed Claude could patent their invention outright. Wrong — it never says patentable. What it actually does is screen the disclosure against six checks before you spend a lawyer's hour on it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A skill is a folder on disk — this one's called invention-intake. Inside sits one file, SKILL.md, written in plain English. No branching, no compiled logic. Claude reads it, then acts. They chose auditability over cleverness: the file is the program, and every step can be pointed at.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The mechanism is deliberately linear. Six screens run in the same order every time — novelty, obviousness, eligibility under §101, bar dates, detectability of infringement, strategic value — then the skill hands back one of three verdicts. No branching, no re-ordering; the order is the contract.

phases.label: Six screens
phases.desc: novelty, obviousness, §101, bar dates, detectability, value

beats.narration_text: One constraint is worth pulling apart. Run all six screens, hand back pursue, investigate, or decline — and never the word patentable. They optimized for a triage the founder can act on in an afternoon at the expense of a legal opinion: patentable is a call that needs a prior-art search and a registered attorney, and this skill is neither.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I've built something I might want to patent. Before I hire a lawyer, walk me through what a well-run invention-intake screen actually checks — novelty against the closest prior art, non-obviousness under a Graham v. Deere lens, subject-matter eligibility under §101, bar-date exposure, whether infringement would even be detectable from a product in the wild, and whether the strategic value survives a design-around. For each check, tell me what a good evidence bundle looks like, what result pushes me toward pursue, investigate, or decline, and what genuinely needs a registered patent attorney. Then ask me your first question. Go deeper: how does the analysis shift for a software or algorithm invention versus hardware or biotech — where do §101 eligibility and detectability change the math?

llm_exercise.prompt: I've built something I might want to patent. Before I hire a lawyer, walk me through what a well-run invention-intake screen actually checks: (1) novelty against the closest prior art — what counts as prior art and where you'd look; (2) non-obviousness under a Graham v. Deere lens — the specific factors and how you weigh them; (3) subject-matter eligibility under §101 — what falls out as an abstract idea or a law of nature; (4) bar-date exposure — the US 1-year grace period versus absolute-novelty regimes abroad, and what public disclosures start the clock; (5) whether infringement would even be detectable from a product in the wild; and (6) whether the strategic value survives a design-around. For each check, tell me what a good evidence bundle looks like, what result would push me toward pursue, investigate, or decline, and what genuinely needs a registered patent attorney versus what I can honestly self-assess. Then ask me your first question so we can screen a real disclosure.
